body: A man is sitting in a launderette at nine in the evening with thirty-five minutes left on the dryer and nothing to do with them. The strip light hums. He takes his phone out to find something to listen to, and the first thing that happens is a card form. He backs out of it. The next one offers a week free and then a monthly charge in smaller type underneath. He backs out of that too, puts the phone face down on the folding table and watches the drum go round instead. It was never that he could not afford it. He was not going to start an arrangement with anybody at nine at night in a launderette.

That small moment happens all day, everywhere, and nobody counts it. A person wanted something ordinary and good, met a form, and decided it was not worth the transaction. Nothing was refused. A door was left a little too heavy to push.
Every station on this band is free to listen to. There is no subscription tier, no advert between songs and no pledge week. You open the page, you press play, and it plays.

That is easy to promise and hard to keep, so it is worth setting out why it can be kept here. Internet radio is normally crushed between two costs. The first is licensing: every play of every song owes a fee to a rights body, and that fee arrives whether ten people are listening or ten thousand, which is why such a service must eventually sell you a subscription or sell your attention to somebody else. The second is production — the studios, the presenters, the engineers, the artwork, the hours. Most services that begin free are running on somebody else’s money until one of those two bills catches up.

This band does not carry the first cost at all. The music was made for this band and is owned outright by the ministry, so there is no per-play fee sitting between a song and the person who needs to hear it. The second cost has been collapsed rather than dodged, and how that was done is its own article. What is left is bandwidth and machines — the one bill in this business that gets cheaper every year instead of dearer.

So free is not a launch promotion here. It is what is left once you remove the two costs that normally force a price. That distinction matters more than it sounds, because a promotional free thing is a decision somebody can reverse on a Tuesday when the numbers look tight, and a structural free thing is not a decision at all. Nobody here has to hold the line every quarter. There is no line to hold. The economics were arranged so that the cheap option and the right option are the same option, which is the only arrangement that survives a hard year.

It is worth saying why this feels unusual. The ordinary experience of the internet now is that everything good is a trial, and the pattern is so familiar it has stopped registering: the first taste is free, the habit forms, and the price appears at exactly the moment leaving would cost you something. It is not fraud and mostly not even cynicism — it is what a business does when its costs rise with every additional listener. But it has trained a generation to flinch at a play button, and that flinch is expensive for anybody with something to give away.

The band is arranged like a broadcast band rather than a catalogue, which matters to the economics as well as the listening. Every station holds one permanent frequency. Nothing is gated behind a tier, because there are no tiers, and no frequency is held back for people who pay. Of the 121 frequencies assigned, 46 are live and playing right now, and the rest are assigned and in build — which is a different sentence from the one a paywall makes.
None of that means nothing is being spent. It means the spending does not scale with you.

Consider the alternative fairly, because the subscription model is not wicked and it solved a real problem. It pays artists. It killed a great deal of piracy. It hands a listener an enormous library for roughly the price of one record a month, which by any reasonable measure is good value. But it does one thing structurally that no goodwill inside the company can undo: it sorts listeners by card. A service funded per head must in the end be built for the heads that can pay, in the countries where cards work. That is not a moral failure. It is arithmetic, and it is why so much of the world hears whatever happens to be free instead.
A gospel that has to clear a payment screen is not going into all the world.

In a village hall on a Sunday morning a woman is setting out eleven small chairs in a semicircle and one for herself. She has run this group for nine years. There is a Bluetooth speaker belonging to her son, a folding table with the biscuits on it, and a heater that takes twenty minutes. She uses her own phone for the music because the group has no budget for anything, and the church has no budget line for her either. Last winter the app she had been using changed something and the songs stopped playing unless she signed in on a plan, so for a few weeks the children sang unaccompanied while she held the tune herself, and she never mentioned it to anybody.

There is no version of that story where the payment screen is doing good work. It sat between eleven children and some music, in a room where everything else had been provided by somebody for nothing.

Now the honest part, because free does not mean unlimited and it would be dishonest to let the word do more work than it can. You will not hear the artists you already like. There is no chart music here and there never will be, because the moment a licensed track plays the per-play fee is back and the structure above collapses. Some frequencies are still in build. The catalogue is one ministry’s catalogue, which means it has a shape, and that shape will not suit everybody who arrives.

But that limitation is not the price of being free. It is the mechanism. The reason there is no card form is the same reason there is no chart music: the songs are owned outright, so nothing has to be collected at the door. You are not being handed a stripped-down version of a paid product while somebody works out how to charge you later. You are being handed a different thing, built by people who decided at the start which of the two they were making and arranged the costs to match.

So the claim is narrow, and it is meant to be. Nobody can promise what the world looks like in ten years. What can be said is that the two bills which normally force a price are not on this ledger, that the one remaining bill falls every year, and that nothing in the design depends on a listener eventually paying. That is a structural argument rather than a pledge, and a structural argument is the only kind worth trusting when somebody tells you a thing will stay free.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. All of it opens the same way, which is to say immediately.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 360.30 — God’s Little Lambs. It is Bible songs and instrumentals for the youngest listeners, warm enough that the adults in the room do not reach to turn it down, and it is the frequency where everything this article has argued becomes concrete. Children’s music is where a paywall bites hardest and least visibly, because it is wanted most by the households with least room in the month and by volunteers running rooms on nothing. Put it on in a village hall, a car, a kitchen at half past seven in the morning. Nothing will interrupt to ask who you are, and nothing will stop in three weeks because a trial ended.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, because an offer is a thing with terms attached and this has none to read. Do not evaluate it and do not sign up for it. Open HM 360.30 this afternoon in whatever room the children are in, and see how far you get before anything asks you for something. That is the entire test, it takes about four seconds, and it is the only claim in this article you do not have to take anybody’s word for.
